 Ontario’s minimum wage is adjusted annually based on the province’s Consumer Price Index (CPI).
 Dreamstime 
 Make us a preferred source on Google 
 By  Soma Ray-Ellis Employment Law Columnist 
 Soma Ray-Ellis is a partner and chair of the employment law group at Toronto law firm Gardiner Roberts LLP. Send your employment law questions to soma@thestar.ca 
 Q: I’m a minimum wage earner in Ontario, and my pay has recently gone up. Can I expect it to keep increasing annually? 
 A: Ontario’s minimum wage rates are subject to annual increases based on the rate of inflation measured through the province’s Consumer Price Index (CPI). Minimum wage is the lowest amount an employer is allowed to pay a worker by law.
 This index measures changes in the cost of goods and services purchased by Ontario consumers, including food, transportation and shelter.
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW 
 Ontario’s minimum wage is adjusted annually based on the CPI. The government announces the new rate by April 1, and the new rate takes effect on Oct. 1.
 This year, as you’ve mentioned, minimum wage has increased.
 Who is impacted by minimum wage increases and what are the new rates?
 The Ontario government states that about 35 per cent of minimum wage workers are employed in the retail trade sector, while about 24 per cent work in accommodation and food services.
 Overall, there are four categories of workers affected by minimum wage hikes in Ontario.
 The first is general minimum wage workers, which includes employees in the retail trade, accommodation, and food services sectors.
 As of Oct. 1, 2026, their wage has increased to $17.95 per hour from $17.60 per hour.
 The second category is student minimum wage, which applies to students younger than 18 who work 28 hours a week or less while school is in session, or work during school breaks or summer holidays.
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW 
 Their wage has increased to $16.90 per hour from $16.60 per hour.
 The third category covers employees who work as hunting, fishing and wilderness guides.
 A wilderness guide is an employee who guides, assists or teaches groups/individuals participating in activities in the wilderness.
 This includes backcountry skiing, snowshoeing, canoeing, hiking and survival training.
 Wages for this group are based on blocks of time rather than by the hour.
 Their rate for working less than five consecutive hours in a day is now $89.75, up from $88.05.
 Their rate for working five or more hours in a day is now $179.50, up from $176.15.
 The last group of minimum wage earners to receive a rate hike are homeworkers.
 A homeworker is defined as an employee who is paid to perform work in their own home.
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW 
 This includes those who write software for a high-tech company, call centre employees, and employees who sew for a manufacturer.
 Their rate is now $19.70 per hour, up from $19.35 per hour.
 Keep in mind that students of all ages employed in this category must receive the homeworker’s minimum wage.
 Key takeaways
 Ontario maintains the second-highest minimum wage rate among provinces in Canada, second to British Columbia, where it is $18.25 per hour.
 If a minimum wage increase comes into effect partway through an employee’s pay period, it will be treated as two separate pay periods, and the employee will be entitled to at least the minimum wage that applies in each of them.
 Additionally, if an employee’s pay is based wholly or partly on commission, it must amount to at least the minimum wage for each hour the employee has worked.
